name: Motion-comp. catheter
full_name: Harvard motion-compensation catheter system (voice-coil guidewire drive with 3-D ultrasound servoing)
group: Harvard SEAS BioRobotics Lab (R. D. Howe; S. B. Kesner)
versions: 2011 ICRA force control of flexible catheter robots for beating-heart surgery (title); 2011 TRO position control with friction and backlash compensation (full, PMC author manuscript); 2014 IJRR robotic catheter cardiac ablation combining 3DUS guidance and force control, new force-sensing RF ablation end effector (full, kesner2014_robotic)
target_anatomy: intracardiac beating-heart repair (mitral annulus tracking); RF cardiac ablation (kesner2014 Sec. 1-2)
devices_driven: guidewire/instrument sliding in a fixed 85 cm Teflon sheath with steel spring; in vivo 1.5 mm OD guidewire in 1.6 mm ID sheath (TRO 2011 Sec. III, Table I)
n_dof_detail: 1 actuated (fast axial translation); bending and rotation by the clinician with conventional catheter controls
translation_detail: other: voice-coil linear actuator (H2W NCC20-18-02-1X, 50.8 mm travel, 26.7 N peak) on a BX3-3 linear ball slide
rotation_detail: none (manual); pull-wire bending and guidewire twisting proposed as future DOF (Fig. 18)
device_range: sheath ID 1.59-2.38 mm with guidewire OD 0.76-2.23 mm tested (Table I)
force_sensing: LCFD-1KG load cell (10 N range) in the drive measures friction; LP-50F potentiometer for position (TRO 2011); IJRR 2014: catheter-tip force sensor, a reflective surface on perpendicular 0.25 mm NiTi flexures read by a fibre-optic transducer, 3D-printed (Objet Connex500), about 5 mm diameter, integrated with the RF ablation electrode, calibrated against an ATI Mini40 (Sec. 2.2, Figs. 4-5)
haptics_leader: linear joystick adds commands to the fast axis; no force feedback reported
imaging_compat: 3-D ultrasound (Philips SONOS 7500, epicardial) with GPU Radon-transform tool tracking; EKF compensates 50-100 ms imaging delay
validation_detail: one 75 kg pig, catheter inserted through the top of the left atrium (not through the vasculature), mitral-annulus tracking trials longer than 15 s; number of trials N.R. (TRO 2011 Sec. VII); IJRR 2014: bench force-control runs and water-tank runs under 3DUS against a target moving 12 mm at about 1 Hz (sinusoid and human mitral-annulus trajectory), robotic vs manual Medtronic RF Marinr MCXL catheter (Sec. 4-5, Figs. 16-17)
key_numbers: in vivo RMS tracking error below 1.0 mm in all trials (0.77 mm shown) vs above 8 mm without compensation; friction compensation up to 2 N; bench MAE 1.28 -> 0.26 mm (inverse compensation, 1 Hz) and 2.34 -> 0.24 mm (model-based); design targets >= 20 mm travel, >= 210 mm/s, >= 3800 mm/s^2, about 4 N (TRO 2011); IJRR 2014: 1 N contact force held on the moving target under 3DUS with 0.08 N RMS error, 97 % less RMS contact-resistance variation than the manual catheter, force control improved motion tracking by about 20 % (Abstract)
